remained unclear. We conducted a study using the ALMA telescope to examine a
representative sample of 14 Class 0 protostars in the Taurus molecular cloud,
focusing on molecular line spectra of $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO around 3 mm in
velocity space. Our analysis revealed that molecular outflows can be classified
into three distinct types: (1) jet-dominated low-velocity patterns, (2)
symmetric low-velocity patterns, and (3) jet-absent low-velocity patterns.
Jet-dominated low-velocity patterns are typically associated with high-speed jets,
whereas symmetric and jet-absent low-velocity patterns are generally not.
Moreover, jet-absent low-velocity patterns are distinguished from symmetric low-
velocity patterns by the presence of a velocity gradient in $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO
spectra, with the former exhibiting a more pronounced gradient.
Jet-absent low-velocity patterns are more prevalent than jet-dominated low-
velocity patterns, suggesting that high-speed jets do not always contribute to
molecular out

This research focuses on developing a control strategy for a specific type of biological process known as the glycolytic oscillator in yeast cells. We aim to identify regulatory conditions that maintain high levels of cell division while ensuring the system remains stable and efficient. By utilizing mathematical modeling and analysis, we discovered that two specific factors are essential for achieving this balance: high concentrations of inorganic phosphate and an appropriate ATP/ADP ratio. Our findings provide a formal explanation for previously observed biological observations and provide a foundation for understanding how biological systems maintain stability and efficiency.

Orbiting satellites experience a variety of orbital perturbations, most notably solar radiation pressure, which can significantly impact their trajectories. Over time, certain characteristics of the orbits change in a predictable manner, as demonstrated by secular equations. This study focuses on identifying new features within the complex equations governing the evolution of orbital parameters under solar radiation pressure. By applying analytical methods to derive approximate solutions and developing a novel approach to obtain exact solutions, this work contributes to the understanding of this phenomenon. The outcomes are visualized and compared to existing models in order to provide a deeper insight into the dynamics of resonances that arise as a result of these mathematical expressions.

Recent advancements in machine-learned functionals of the wavefields have shown great promise in emulating light-matter interactions within realistic models derived from first principles. For these models to be efficiently solved with minimal resources, it's essential to employ localized basis functions. However, most existing models assume a periodic potential, resulting in electrons' Bloch states with measure invariance. This characteristic makes the numerical solution of interacting electrons cumbersome. Although a method to address this issue has been proposed, it's primarily suitable for weakly-coupled systems. In this work, we propose a framework to derive a localized tight-binding Hamiltonian for strongly-coupled systems of light and matter. By applying a unitary transformation to the Bloch basis, we render the photons' basis unitarily equivalent. This enables the application of machine-learned functionals in resource-constrained environments.

Our focus is on object recognition within a specific, pre-defined set of categories (e.g., basic shapes or everyday items like cups). We achieve this through training on a combination of 2D images with aligned keypoints and 3D models with corresponding vertices. Our approach utilizes the distinct characteristics of these datasets to their full potential. By leveraging 3D information, we enhance the robustness of our keypoint-based matching process to handle variations in object appearance, thus improving performance in real-world applications. Conversely, by training on 2D images, we gain a better understanding of object poses, which in turn facilitates more accurate form reconstruction from a single image. We've tested our approach on various real-world object classes and achieved superior results on multiple benchmarks.

This project addresses the INSTAT lab issue by employing Monte Carlo simulations to determine the coverage probability of standard, data-dependent 95% confidence intervals for a sample of n data points drawn from a Cauchy distribution with parameters (θ1, θ2), where θ1 represents the center and θ2 represents the scale. We specifically calculate probability squares for these parameters. The study utilizes the method of maximum likelihood estimation to estimate the parameters and employs Wilson-Hunter estimation to calculate the confidence intervals for the cauchy distribution's parameters.

A type of clinical trial known as platform trials is used to evaluate multiple treatments against a shared control group, and one variant of these trials, the basket trial, groups patients by similarity and tests them in B arms simultaneously. By utilizing statistical methods that analyze responses from trial arms in combination, we can gain insights into the potential efficacy of treatments. This research applies a Bayesian approach to determine an appropriate sample size for such trials, taking into account the shared control arm and any observed responses. Through simulations, we assess the accuracy of this method and compare it to traditional planning methods. Ultimately, we illustrate the practical application of our approach using a planned pediatric trial.

A recent research project developed a control strategy known as the sequential loop shutting technique to optimize motion systems with precise movements. Multiple studies have utilized this technique to simplify complex feedback control by breaking it down into manageable segments. Our work builds upon these studies by refining the method through customized filter and gain calculations. We first refined a second-order system model to accurately represent the motion system being controlled. We then incorporated this improved model into the existing SLS framework. We also introduced an additional filter to further enhance the performance of the motion control system. This approach was demonstrated with a nanometer-accurate stage, which showed significant improvements in both settling time and residual motion compared to the original SLS technique.

Our focus is on the challenging task of partial-to-full shape correspondence recovery under significant occlusion. Our proposed method, PRNet, utilizes a recurrent neural network to iteratively refine predictions of partial shape correspondence. Building upon the popular DeepGlobal approach, PRNet's design draws inspiration from traditional image segmentation methods, incorporating a network that simultaneously captures local and global features. A key component of PRNet is a self-guided learning mechanism that enables it to adapt to input partial shapes and produce coherent correspondence. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's superiority over DeepGlobal in achieving improved IoU scores for the ShapeNet benchmark.

The $R_\infty$ characteristic is identified as a significant invariant in studying inverse limits of groups with a common finite $G_n$ quotient, where the characteristic holds constant under such limits. In the specific case of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups (gsbs), the number of finite quotients exhibiting the $R_\infty$ characteristic is limited to two distinct classes: those exhibiting a $\mathbb{Z}^2$ second homology group and those exhibiting a $\mathbb{Z}$ rank in the same invariant.

Recent research by the Topological Vector Meson Dominance model suggests that the Standard Model vacuum decays after approximately $10^{10}$ years, largely due to the Higgs field settling at a deeper, stable minimum. A precise measurement of the self-coupling parameter is crucial for understanding the true nature of the instability and verifying non-minimal Standard Model extensions. Currently, direct production of relevant particles at future colliders is unfeasible due to their high masses. Instead, we propose that future colliders can create conditions to create new vacuum bubbles, which can be studied through their multi-jet signatures. Specifically, a 100 TeV collider has the potential to directly measure the self-coupling parameter, while a 33 TeV collider could at least set a stringent upper limit on its value.

A new method is developed for inverse problems by applying the gradient of an optimal control problem to iterative reconstruction. A dynamic programming approach based on Bellman's principle is used to derive the gradient via differentiation of the control problem, avoiding the need for adjoint-state equations. The strategy on offer, the trajectory framework, is a versatile framework that can be applied to a range of problems and does not rely on adjoint-state equations. The method is successfully applied to the tomographic reconstruction of time-sensitive data, using both artificial and real data from a micro-focus X-ray CT scanner. The results show the proposed approach's stability and robustness in handling such problems.

We calculate the vector and axial vector charmed mesons' ($D^*$, $D^*_s$) GPDs, 
light-front wave functions, and light-front wave functions squared using lattice QEC 
distributions, and use them to derive the parton model densities of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ 
mesons. Our findings for the percent-level contributions from sea quarks are 
consistent with phenomenological models.

We derive precise conditions for the weighted Fourier transform to be a bijective map with a continuous inverse from $S^{\gamma}$ to $S^{\beta}_b$, where $b$ denotes a sequence with specific properties, when certain inequalities involving $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are met. This result enables us to investigate under what conditions the Toeplitz operators with exponential-type symbols are invertible with a bounded inverse.

In the realm of semi-supervised learning, leveraging multiple data modalities can greatly expand the labeling scope and enhance model performance. Recent breakthroughs in cross-domain generative adversarial networks have enabled instantaneous adaptation to novel domains; however, these methods often struggle when dealing with diverse modalities due to substantial mode discrepancies. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that partitions instances across modalities at a granular level through a cyclic division process. By integrating conditional generative adversarial networks and adversarial instance classification, our method facilitates domain-generalization without relying mode-specific information. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our method outperforms current SOTA approaches that deal with multi-modalities by a significant margin of 3.16% average improvement across various models and domain combinations.

To enhance long sequence analysis, our proposed method combines an existing model with a new feature extraction technique, specifically a differential optimizer and unique node initializations in a Long Short-Term Memory network. This approach model, RKFM-LSTM, utilizes Radial Basis Function kernelized feature mapping to efficiently map high-dimensional spaces and automatically determine the optimal number of nodes in the model, while the RKFM itself is combined with LSTM to effectively capture temporal dependencies in action prediction tasks. In addition, our model's performance is further improved by integrating an L2 regularization model to mitigate overfitting and utilizing a BA-DASO model for parameter optimization, which significantly reduces the computational cost while maintaining high performance. As demonstrated by experimental results, our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on two widely used action recognition datasets, specifically UCF101-24 and JHMDB-21.

A new study has simulated NRN disk winds from the massive star AD Leo to explain its massive UV continuum eruption in 1985. This star, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, experienced a significant increase in continuum flux across a wide spectrum, ranging from 3200 to 31,000 Angstroms. Previous research suggested that luminous blue variable stars are responsible for such eruptions, but this star is not classified as an LBV. This star's properties were modeled using MHD simulations, which showed that the simulation accurately matched the observed flux at most wavelengths. This simulation also revealed the characteristic spatial and temporal properties of disk winds, which may be observable through interferometry. This study provides a starting point for further research into the physical processes behind such eruptions, which are common among massive stars.

We are investigating the deformations of G2-instantons defined on nearly G2 manifolds. Our approach involves establishing a precise relationship between the linearized deformation of a G2-instanton on a nearly G2 structure and the deformation of the underlying G2 metric.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is termed $C$-normal if it satisfies the equation $TC^*T=C^*TC^*$. The purpose of this paper is to investigate the $C$-normal weighted composition operator $W_\phi C_{\psi, T}$ acting on the Hardy space $H^2$, where $C$ is the Cesaro operator.

A partition's A-core is its A'-belian component. We've analyzed the distribution of A-cores of partitions whose parts are all less than or equal to P. Utilizing a stochastic model based on random walks, we found the probabilities of a given A-core occurring. Notably, these results align with the combinatorial compositions of A-core elements. Furthermore, the variance of the number of cores decreases exponentially as the partition's total increases.

Our research focuses on enhancing point cloud learning by exploring various geometric transformations that improve the quality of the data representation, a crucial aspect often overlooked in existing studies. To address the representation problem, we propose a novel approach, TPC, a PointNet-based feature extractor that takes multiple transformed point clouds as input to produce high-quality features. Since the optimal geometric transformation varies across different scenarios, TPC is a flexible framework that can accommodate any set of transformed point clouds as input. Moreover, we employ a novel unsupervised learning method to determine the optimal transformation parameters, a key component of our approach. Through our experiments on multiple datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in point cloud classification, segmentation, and surface reconstruction.

In the FMCW radar technology, it is possible to gather a vast amount of data within a very short time frame. This can lead to high interference between radar signals due to data range and DC offset issues. To address this problem, this research investigates methods to minimize interference in a group of FMCW radars using MAC protocols like slotted ALOHA, carrier sense multiple access (CSMA), and compares them through simulations. The best outcome from this research could contribute to the development of autonomous vehicle systems and other 3G/4G/5G wireless applications.

This study evaluates experiments involving Hong-Ou-Mandel interference that have investigated the phenomenon of Absorption induced by Stimulated Emission of Radiation in two-photon processes using OPO sources. Two specific experiments are here analyzed in detail with the aid of spectral measurements. One such experiment is by Mathew et al., employing a type-II degenerate optical parametric oscillator and a sample doped with Tb ions in a lattice, while another experiment utilizes a similar source but with a YIG sample doped with Cr ions. By utilizing a 2D code written in MATLAB, we have been able to verify the results that were reported in these experiments. Three-dimensional codes written in both MATLAB and Python are also presented that provide a visual representation of the underlying physical phenomena.
